study.title: Psalm 106 - Confession of Israel's guilt and appeal for restoration
study.overview: Psalm 106 is a song of praise that does not ignore the sin of the people. He begins and ends with "Aleluia," but in the middle makes a long and humble confession of Israel's rebellion throughout its history. The psalm recalls unbelief in Egypt, the murmurings in the wilderness, idolatry, the resistance to the leaders raised up by God, and infidelity in the promised land. Still, he points out that the Lord acted repeatedly because of his name, his covenant and his mercy. The closing transforms the memory of the past into prayer: "Pave us, Lord our God, and gather us from among the nations," followed by a doxology that affirms the eternity of the Lord and summons all the people to the "Am."

outline.title: Called to praise and prayer for divine favor
outline.explanation: The psalm opens with adoration to the Lord for his permanent goodness and for his powerful works, and soon passes into a personal supplication: the psalmist asks that God remember him and include him in the joy of his people and his inheritance. Praise is not abstract; it is born of the desire to share in salvation and the good granted to the chosen ones.

outline.title: Confession of ancient sins: unbelief, murmuring, and idolatry
outline.explanation: Here the people recognize that they have sinned like their parents. The text passes through Egypt, the Red Sea, the desert and the Horeb, showing a repeated pattern: God saves, the people forget, complains, desires what is bad and falls into idolatry. Even so, the Lord delivers because of his name and intervenes through Moses not to completely destroy the people.

outline.title: Rejection of promise, contamination with nations and persistent mercy
outline.explanation: The psalm continues with the refusal to rely on God's word on the promised land, the rebellion in Kadesh, the association with peoples and idols, and extreme acts of corruption, including child sacrifices. The result is severe discipline: oppression, humiliation and captivity. Still, God looks at anguish, hears the cry, remembers his covenant and moves even the oppressors to favor his people.

outline.title: Final prayer for conclusive gathering and doxology
outline.explanation: The conclusion unites request and worship. The people ask God to save and bring him up among the nations so that he can give thanks to his holy name. The psalm ends blessing the Lord, stating that he reigns forever and calls all the people to answer with "Amém" and "Aleluia."

study.context: The notes provided indicate that the psalm was associated by some interpreters with the time of exile and dispersion, because the final prayer asks for assembling among the nations. It is also observed that parts of the initial and final verses appear in 1 Chronicles 16. This backdrop is plausible by the notes, but it is not presented here as a closed conclusion, only as an interpretive possibility.
study.theology: The Psalm teaches that the history of God's people is marked by two inseparable axes: the constant fidelity of the Lord and the recurring infidelity of man. The goodness of God is not annulled by the sin of the people; on the contrary, it stands out even more. The text shows that salvation comes because of the name of God, his mercy and his covenant, not because Israel deserves it. At the same time, sin has real consequences: unbelief, discipline, dispersion and oppression. There is also a strong theology of memory: forgetting the works of God leads to rebellion, while remembering them sustains repentance, praise and hope. The psalm still presents intercession: Moses puts himself in the loop, and Fineias intervenes, pointing out that God raises mediators and agents of preservation in the midst of judgment. Finally, the desired restoration is not only political or territorial; it aims at the gratitude and glory of the holy name of the Lord.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm depicts the community in exile confessing the Lord's goodness, the very historical sinfulness and asking to be gathered back from the places to which it was scattered; the final hope is in God's renewed mercy.

The psalm begins and ends in praise because even sorrow for sin should not take the people out of the tone of worship; the confession of sin serves to justify God's righteousness and feed hope in his mercy.

The final doxology expresses gratitude for what God has already made and confidence that he will complete the restoration; the call to the "Amém" invites all the people to unite in prayer and thanksgiving.

questions: What sins of spiritual forgetfulness appear most often in my life: ingratitude, murmuring, disorderly desire or trust in modern idols?
How can the memory of God's works be transformed not only my praise, but also my repentance and my practical decisions?
How can I share today in prayer by gathering, restoration, and witnessing of the holy name of the Lord in the community of faith?
study.practice: This week, read the psalm slowly and mark every time the people "squece," "murmura" or "be rebel," then write alongside each failure a concrete memory of God's fidelity in their lives. Then pray verse 47 with your own words, asking for personal and community restoration, and practice visible gratitude: thank God aloud and share with another person a specific act of his goodness.
study.uncertainty: The notes allow us to associate the psalm with the period of exile, but do not require this dating; nor do they allow to affirm with certainty authorship of David. Internal historical allusions are clear, but some references of the psalm are summarized poetically and depend on the broader biblical memory. The voices of the commentators were maintained as interpretations, not as absolute definitions of the meaning of the text.
